modalities.name: Caring Off the Clock
modalities.tagline: A short rest from wishing anyone well, yourself included.
modalities.whatItIs: Caring Off the Clock is a new, untested idea that takes Do Nothing meditation in the opposite direction from loving-kindness practice. Instead of sending warm wishes to yourself and others, you sit alone with your eyes open, hold no one in mind on purpose and make no effort to feel anything in particular toward anybody.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta builds warm feeling on purpose with set phrases and pictured faces; this goes the other way, with no phrases, no faces and no feeling to produce, so that people who spend all day caring can rest from the effort of it. Whatever mood is already there, warm, flat or irritable, is left as it is.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit somewhere ordinary, alone, for 15 to 20 minutes with your eyes open and resting loosely on the room. When someone you look after comes to mind, you neither send them good wishes nor make plans for them, and you let the thought pass like a sound outside. If you notice a wish to feel kinder, calmer or better, you let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: Carers, parents, nurses and anyone who feels they must be warm and attentive all the time and would like a few minutes off duty.
modalities.cautions: If worry about someone is urgent, deal with it first, and if numbness or not caring about anything lasts for weeks, it can be a sign of burnout or depression worth raising with a doctor. Like any meditation it can stir up difficult feelings, so people with severe depression, trauma or dissociation should practice with a clinician's support.
modalities.tweet: Loving-kindness asks you to send warm wishes. Caring Off the Clock is a new concept that asks for nothing: 15 minutes alone, eyes open, no wishes sent to anyone, no feeling to produce. A short break from caring, meant for carers, parents and nurses. Untested.

modalities.name: No Levels, No Records
modalities.tagline: Every sit counts the same, and nothing is kept.
modalities.whatItIs: No Levels, No Records is a new, untested idea that pushes Do Nothing meditation away from concentration practices that build skill toward special states. There is no teacher, no object, no stage to reach and no log. If a lovely or unusual state turns up, you do not try to hold it or get it back next time.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana is a long-term skill with stages, mastery and a teacher; this goes the other way, so that meditation can never become a ladder to climb or a performance to measure. Each sit counts the same, however it went.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone for 10 to 20 minutes and let whatever happens happen, without choosing anything to focus on or trying to go deeper. Afterward you write nothing down and rate nothing, and if you catch yourself trying to repeat a good sit or avoid a bad one, you let that wish go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have turned meditation into another goal to achieve, or who feel they are always doing it wrong.
modalities.cautions: With no anchor and no teacher some people drift, doze or slide into worry, so keep sits short and stop if they leave you more upset than before. Strong fear, unusual perceptions or a changed sense of self during or after sitting are reasons to stop and talk to a clinician, and people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, dissociation or severe trauma should get advice before meditating on their own.
modalities.tweet: Meditation without a scoreboard. No Levels, No Records is a proposed practice: sit for 10 to 20 minutes, aim for nothing, write nothing down, and if a lovely state shows up, don't chase it next time. Every sit counts the same. Untested, so go gently.

modalities.name: Still Body, Roaming Mind
modalities.tagline: Settle the body once, then let it drop out of view.
modalities.whatItIs: Still Body, Roaming Mind is a new, untested idea that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as it can go from dancing: no movement, no music, no company and no attention to the body. You settle yourself once, lying fully supported, and then leave your thoughts and daydreams free to go wherever they go.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance lets feeling out through movement, rhythm and other people; this goes the opposite way, letting the body go so quiet that it drops out of attention while the mind roams unsupervised. Thinking is not treated as a failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: Take a few minutes to get fully comfortable lying on a bed or sofa, with pillows under your head and knees and a blanket, so there is nothing left to adjust. Then, for 20 minutes, alone and in silence, you let thoughts, plans and daydreams run as they like, without scanning or following the body. If you notice an effort to stop thinking or clear the mind, you drop it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body-focused relaxation uncomfortable or dull, and people who believe meditation means emptying the mind and would like permission not to.
modalities.cautions: A roaming mind can drift into worry or painful memories, so if it keeps circling one distressing thing, get up and do something else, and anyone with severe depression, trauma or a tendency to dissociate should talk to a clinician first. You may fall asleep, so do not try it when you need to stay alert.
modalities.tweet: What if meditation let you think as much as you like? Still Body, Roaming Mind is an untested idea: get fully comfortable lying down, stop minding your body, and let thoughts and daydreams wander for 20 minutes. If it turns into worry, simply get up.

modalities.name: Temperature, As Found
modalities.tagline: Real warmth and coolness in the body, watched and left alone.
modalities.whatItIs: Temperature, As Found is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from loving-kindness. Where metta pictures warmth spreading from the heart toward people, this sit watches only the body's actual temperatures, its warm and cool spots, as they change, without trying to warm anything up.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta adds an imagined, chosen warmth; going the other way, attention stays with plain, real sensation and adds nothing, not even kindness. Temperature suits this well because it keeps shifting with the breath, with contact and with the air.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 30 minutes in an ordinary room and move attention through the body in a fixed order: nostrils and lips, hands, the backs of the legs where they touch the seat, then the feet. At each place you stay for a few breaths and feel whether it is warm, cool or neither and how that shifts, such as cool air coming in at the nose and warmer air going out, then move on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who find kindness practices forced or sugary and want something plainer, and anyone curious to see how constantly ordinary sensations change.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to the body can make some people anxious or bring up uncomfortable sensations, so open your eyes, move or stop if it becomes distressing. Longer or retreat-style practice can bring up difficult experiences, so learn from a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties, and people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first.
modalities.tweet: Instead of imagining warmth, notice the warmth that is already there. Temperature, As Found is a new meditation idea: 30 minutes moving through the body, feeling warm and cool spots shift with each breath, and leaving them alone. Plain and untested.

modalities.name: Rope Between Two
modalities.tagline: Short, all-out rope pulls against a real partner's real force.
modalities.whatItIs: Rope Between Two is a new, untested idea for interval training in pairs, in which two people of similar size pull against each other on a short, thick rope in hard 15-second bouts. It pushes interval training further from loving-kindness: instead of wishing someone well in your mind, you meet a real person's force with your own, as hard as you both can, and then let go.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta sends imagined warmth toward pictured people; going the other way, this is direct, physical contact with another person's effort through a rope, with nothing imagined and no feeling required. Honest effort against honest resistance, then a full release, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, pairs matched by size stand on a grass or matted floor and follow a fixed plan: eight bouts of 15 seconds pulling hard on a short rope from a low, braced stance, each followed by 90 seconds of easy walking. Nobody wins or loses, there is no line to drag anyone over, and either partner can end a bout early by calling 'release', when both ease off slowly rather than letting go suddenly. You finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find gentle, inward practices hard to feel and who would rather meet another person in honest physical effort.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts strain the heart, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or back trouble, always warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Pulling hard can strain the back, shoulders and hands and a sudden let-go can cause falls, so use gloves and a soft surface, match partners by size, never wrap the rope around a hand and always ease off together.
modalities.tweet: Two people, one short rope, eight hard 15-second pulls. Rope Between Two is a new idea: meet a real person's effort with your own, no winner, then ease off together. Untested. Warm up, use gloves and soft ground, and stop at any chest pain or dizziness.

modalities.name: Relay and Roar
modalities.tagline: Flat-out relay legs while everyone else cheers out loud.
modalities.whatItIs: Relay and Roar is a new, untested idea for an evening of short, flat-out relay races in mixed teams, where everyone who is not running cheers out loud for whoever is, on every team. It pushes team sport away from loving-kindness: support is not wished silently in the mind but shown at full volume, in a real crowd.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta builds goodwill quietly, alone and in imagination; going the opposite way, this makes support loud, physical and shared, so that cheering and being cheered happen in the open. Nothing is planned beyond the next race, and the mood is meant to be wild rather than tender.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute group warm-up and a round of names, players form mixed teams of five or six on a grass field and run relay legs of 30 to 60 meters for about 40 minutes, with at least two minutes between each person's turns. The one rule beyond the race is that everyone not running shouts encouragement for each runner by name, including runners on other teams, and teams are reshuffled every few races.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel awkward with gentle, inward kindness practices but light up in a noisy crowd, and anyone who rarely hears their name cheered.
modalities.cautions: Sprinting carries a real risk of hamstring and ankle injuries and strains the heart, so get medical advice first if you have heart or other health conditions, warm up properly, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Being shouted at, even kindly, can feel overwhelming, so anyone may walk a leg or cheer quietly.
modalities.tweet: Picture a field, short relay sprints, and everyone not running shouting your name, even the other teams. Relay and Roar is a proposed practice where support is loud, not silent. Warm up first, walk your leg if you like, and stop for any chest pain.

modalities.name: One Long Hill
modalities.tagline: A single long climb, with the slope setting the effort.
modalities.whatItIs: One Long Hill is a new, untested idea that pushes endurance training away from loving-kindness, toward a hard, real, outdoor challenge that kind words cannot soften. You run, hike or cycle up one long hill, alone and with no plan beyond reaching the top, and let the slope decide how hard you work.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta follows a set script of gentle phrases aimed at imagined people; going the other way, there is no script and no one in mind, only the actual ground rising and the body meeting it. The hill sets the effort, and you take it as it comes.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a long, safe hill or climbing road you know, warm up for 10 to 15 minutes on the flat, then climb without stopping for 20 to 40 minutes, running where you can and walking where it gets steep, with your eyes on the ground a few steps ahead. At the top you stop and look around for a few minutes, then come down slowly and carefully, since descents are where many falls happen.
modalities.whoItsFor: Fairly fit runners, hikers or cyclists who want a simple, wholehearted challenge with no numbers attached.
modalities.cautions: Long hard climbs strain the heart and legs, so check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or joint problems, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Check the weather and the terrain, tell someone your route, carry water and a phone, and turn back if conditions turn bad.
modalities.tweet: An idea: no pace, no playlist, no plan. Just one long hill. Warm up, then climb for 20 to 40 minutes, running where you can and walking where it's steep, and let the slope set the effort. One Long Hill. Check the weather, and see a doctor first if needed.

modalities.name: Heavy and Still
modalities.tagline: Hold a real heavy load still and feel what holding takes.
modalities.whatItIs: Heavy and Still is a new, untested idea that pushes strength training further from loving-kindness. Instead of moving weights up and down, you hold heavy loads still for counted seconds, following a fixed plan, and keep attention on the plain physical feel of gravity pulling and your body holding.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta works with gentle wishes and imagined warmth; going the other way, this is about the most concrete experience of strength there is, a real weight that has to be held, felt directly and with no imagery. The fixed plan leaves nothing to negotiate.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up and some lighter practice, you do three holds: a barbell held just above the knees inside a rack with safety bars, a pair of heavy dumbbells held at your sides, and a wall sit, each for a set 20 to 30 seconds, three times, with 2 to 3 minutes of rest. You add a little load or time each week, and during every hold you breathe steadily and keep attention on the pull of the weight, your grip and your feet.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like strength training but want a simpler, steadier form of it, or whose minds race during exercise and who want something plainly physical to rest attention on.
modalities.cautions: Heavy holds raise blood pressure sharply, especially with breath-holding, so anyone with high blood pressure or heart or eye problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should keep breathing, warm up, use safety bars and learn the positions from a qualified coach. Stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Strength without the reps. Heavy and Still is an untested idea: hold a real heavy load still for 20 to 30 seconds, breathe steadily and feel gravity pull. Learn it from a coach, keep breathing, and check with a doctor first if your blood pressure runs high.

modalities.name: Wait to Be Chosen
modalities.tagline: Sit among the animals and let them decide whether to come.
modalities.whatItIs: Wait to Be Chosen is a new, untested idea for small-group sessions in a field or barn with calm animals, such as sheep, alpacas or horses, led by a trained professional and a handler. You do not call, feed, stroke or try to win over any animal: you sit and watch, and each animal decides for itself whether to come near.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta sends warmth outward on purpose, often toward imagined beings; this goes the other way, toward real animals met as they are and a closeness that cannot be pushed. Letting an animal choose, and being all right if it does not, is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to six people sit quietly on low stools, spread out in a field or large pen, for about an hour. If an animal comes close you stay still and let it sniff or stand beside you, reaching out only if the handler says it is fine. Afterward the professional leads a short talk about wanting to be liked and what it was like to wait.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who try hard to win others over or feel rejected easily, and who would like to practice wanting contact without chasing it.
modalities.cautions: Large animals can kick, butt or knock people over, so the handler picks calm animals, sets distances and can end the session, and people with allergies or a fear of animals should say so first. The animals must always be free to move away, have water and shelter and never be lured or crowded, and if being ignored by an animal stirs strong feelings of rejection, the professional should be ready to talk it through.
modalities.tweet: Sit in a field with sheep or alpacas and do nothing to win them over: no calling, no food, no reaching out. Wait to Be Chosen is a new concept about wanting contact without chasing it, led by a professional. The animals stay free to walk away.

modalities.name: One-Legged Slow Form
modalities.tagline: A slow form on one leg, where every wobble is real.
modalities.whatItIs: One-Legged Slow Form is a new, untested idea that takes qigong further from loving-kindness, away from imagined warmth and toward plain physical feedback. You practice a short, set sequence of slow movements standing on one leg at a time, so balance gives honest, moment-by-moment information that cannot be pictured or wished into place.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta settles the heart through repeated phrases and pictured people; going the other way, this steadies the body through something entirely real and immediate, the act of balancing. Wobbles are allowed and watched, not fought.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher first shows you the form and checks your setup. Then, standing beside a wall or a sturdy chair, you warm up for a few minutes and repeat a short form of four or five slow arm movements, first on the left leg and then on the right, for 20 to 25 minutes in all. When you wobble you touch the wall lightly, notice the feel of the foot, ankle and hips, and carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy qigong but find its imagery vague, and people who want a gentle practice that keeps attention firmly in the body.
modalities.cautions: Standing on one leg brings a risk of falls, so always practice beside a wall or chair on a clear, non-slip floor, and people with balance problems, dizziness, osteoporosis or a history of falls should ask a doctor or physiotherapist first. Stop if you feel dizzy or have joint pain.
modalities.tweet: Qigong without the imagery: a slow, set sequence done on one leg at a time, next to a wall, where every wobble is real feedback. One-Legged Slow Form is a new idea, untested. If falls or dizziness are a concern for you, ask a physio first.

modalities.name: Watching a Taste End
modalities.tagline: A small real pleasure, watched closely as it fades to nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Watching a Taste End is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from concentration absorption. Where jhana builds up pleasure and tries to keep it steady, this practice takes one small, real pleasure, the taste of a sip of tea or a piece of fruit, and watches it change and fade until nothing is left.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana cultivates bliss and learns to stay in it; going the other way, this lets a plain, ordinary pleasure end on its own and keeps attention on the ending. Seeing a good thing pass, closely and without holding on, is the point.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting alone for about 25 minutes in a set routine, you take one sip of a flavorful drink or one small piece of fruit, swallow, close your eyes and follow the taste as it shifts, thins and finally disappears, without taking more to keep it going. When it is fully gone you rest for a minute and notice what is there instead, then repeat, about six times.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who tend to chase or cling to pleasant states, and people who find it hard to let good moments end.
modalities.cautions: Use small amounts of ordinary food or drink, and anyone with an eating disorder or a difficult relationship with food should skip it or check with their clinician first. Like other insight practice it can bring up difficult experiences, so people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before longer or retreat practice.
modalities.tweet: Take one sip of tea, close your eyes, and follow the taste until it's completely gone. Then do it again. Watching a Taste End is a new meditation idea: let a small pleasure end without reaching for more. Untested, and not for anyone with eating difficulties.

modalities.name: Signal Start Sprints
modalities.tagline: Wait alert, then go the instant the signal comes.
modalities.whatItIs: Signal Start Sprints is a new, untested idea that pushes interval training away from concentration absorption, toward wide, outward alertness. You wait with eyes open and attention on the room, and each all-out bout starts only when a light flashes or a beep sounds at an unpredictable moment.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana withdraws from the senses into one inner object and holds it for a long time; going the other way, this keeps attention open, outward and ready for something unpredictable, then turns it into explosive action. The waiting is as much the practice as the sprint.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike, rower or flat track, you follow a fixed plan of eight to ten all-out bouts of 10 to 15 seconds. Each bout is started by a light or sound from an interval app set to go off at a random moment between 60 and 120 seconds after the last one ended, and while waiting you move easily with eyes up and senses open. You finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who drift off in long meditation or steady exercise and want a practice that keeps them alert and responsive for short stretches.
modalities.cautions: All-out efforts strain the heart, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or other conditions, always warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Explosive starts can pull muscles, so keep the first few sessions at moderate effort, and use a sound cue instead of a light if you have photosensitive epilepsy.
modalities.tweet: Stand ready, eyes up, and sprint the moment the signal comes, whenever that is. Signal Start Sprints is a new interval idea built on staying alert rather than zoning out. Untested. Warm up, use a sound cue if lights bother you, stop at any chest pain.

modalities.name: Three-Ball Chaos
modalities.tagline: Three balls in play at once, so nobody can focus on one.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Ball Chaos is a new, untested idea for a fast pickup game with three balls in play at the same time, so players have to keep attention wide and moving instead of narrowing it to one thing. It pushes team sport as far as it goes from concentration absorption: eyes open, constant change, lots of people and no coach.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana narrows attention to a single object, alone and under a teacher's guidance; going the other way, this spreads it across a whole moving field, shared with many players who run the game themselves. Nobody can track everything, and the fun is in letting that be.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, two teams of six to eight play on a grass field with two goals and three soft balls, in 8-minute games with short rests, for about 45 minutes. Any ball can score, players call their own fouls, and at each break teams swap one player and say what was most chaotic.
modalities.whoItsFor: Players who get tense or fixated in competitive games, and people who want a loud, laughing break from tunnel vision.
modalities.cautions: Fast play with several balls raises the risk of collisions and ankle, knee and head injuries, so use soft balls, ban slide tackles, warm up and stop playing after any knock to the head. People with heart or other health conditions should get medical advice first, and anyone with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness stops at once.
modalities.tweet: What if a game had three balls in play at once? Three-Ball Chaos is a proposed pickup game where nobody can watch everything, so attention has to stay wide and loose. Soft balls, self-called fouls, no coach. Warm up first, and stop after any knock to the head.

modalities.name: Landmark to Landmark
modalities.tagline: Pick a point ahead, reach it, then pick the next.
modalities.whatItIs: Landmark to Landmark is a new, untested idea for a hard, unplanned run or ride in which you keep choosing a visible landmark ahead, such as a tree, a gate or a bend, go to it, and then choose the next. It moves endurance training away from concentration absorption, toward attention that keeps landing on new things in the outside world.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana holds one inner object steadily for a long time, usually with a teacher; going the other way, this keeps attention outward and on the move, settling on a new target every minute or two, with no plan and no one guiding. The route builds itself one landmark at a time.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute easy warm-up on paths or quiet roads you know, you go at a hard but steady effort for 30 to 50 minutes, each time picking the next landmark you can see and heading for it, with no set route and no screen to check. When you want to stop, you choose one last landmark that points home and cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners and cyclists who are bored by fixed routes and numbers, and people whose attention tends to sink into worry during long efforts.
modalities.cautions: Hard efforts strain the heart, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Without a planned route it is easy to go too far or get lost, so stay in an area you know, carry a phone and water, tell someone where you are going, and watch the weather and footing.
modalities.tweet: A tree, then a gate, then that bend in the road. Landmark to Landmark is a new idea for a hard run or ride with no planned route: just keep picking the next thing you can see. Stay somewhere you know, carry a phone, and check with a doctor first if needed.

modalities.name: Outward Cue Lifting
modalities.tagline: Lift by pushing the floor away, not by looking inward.
modalities.whatItIs: Outward Cue Lifting is a new, untested idea that pushes strength training away from concentration absorption, toward attention placed entirely outside the body. Every heavy set is done with one simple outward cue, such as pushing the floor away or driving the bar toward the ceiling, instead of attention on muscles, breath or inner states.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana turns attention inward onto one object until the outside world fades; going the other way, this keeps attention on the floor, the bar and the room, and uses them to organize hard effort. The plan is fixed in advance, so the only job during a set is the cue.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week, after a 10-minute warm-up, you follow a written plan of three or four main lifts, such as squats, presses, rows and deadlifts, for 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 6 hard repetitions with 2 to 3 minutes of rest, adding a little weight each week. Before each set you choose one outward cue, such as 'push the floor away' or 'drive the bar to the ceiling', say it once and hold only that in mind until the set ends.
modalities.whoItsFor: Lifters who get lost in their own heads before heavy sets, and people who want a training practice that turns attention outward rather than inward.
modalities.cautions: Heavy lifting raises blood pressure sharply, especially with breath-holding, so people with high blood pressure or heart or eye problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should keep breathing, warm up, use safety bars or a spotter and learn technique from a qualified coach. Stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and lower the weight if your form breaks down.
modalities.tweet: Before each heavy set, pick one cue outside your body, like 'push the floor away', and hold only that in mind. Outward Cue Lifting is a new strength idea: attention on the world, not inside your head. Untested. Learn form from a coach, and keep breathing.

modalities.name: Where the Goat Goes
modalities.tagline: Follow one goat's interests around the field, then swap.
modalities.whatItIs: Where the Goat Goes is a new, untested idea for small-group sessions at a farm or sanctuary in which each person quietly follows one goat around a large enclosure, at a respectful distance, going where it goes and looking at what it looks at. A trained professional and a keeper lead, and the group talks afterward.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana chooses one object and holds attention there, alone; going the other way, this hands the choice of where to look to another creature whose interests keep changing, and shares the experience with others. Attention follows rather than fixes.
modalities.whatYouDo: After the keeper explains goat body language and the distance to keep, four to six people each follow a goat for about 10 minutes, walking slowly, stopping when it stops and noticing what catches its interest, then switch to a different goat, three times in all. The session ends with 20 minutes of conversation, led by the professional, about what it was like to let something else steer your attention.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose attention gets stuck on the same worries or tasks and who would enjoy loosening it in a gentle, outdoor setting with others.
modalities.cautions: Goats can butt, nibble and knock people over, so keep the distance the keeper sets, never corner or chase a goat, and wear sturdy shoes on uneven ground; people with allergies or a fear of animals should say so first. The keeper watches for signs of stress, makes sure the goats always have space to retreat and ends a follow if a goat seems bothered.
modalities.tweet: Follow one goat around a field for ten minutes, look at what it looks at, then swap. Where the Goat Goes is a new concept for letting something else steer your attention, led by a professional and a keeper. The goats can always walk away.

modalities.name: Leaderless Circle Form
modalities.tagline: A slow form done together, eyes open, with nobody in front.
modalities.whatItIs: Leaderless Circle Form is a new, untested idea in which a small group who already know a qigong form practice it standing in a circle, facing inward with eyes open, keeping together by watching each other rather than following a teacher. It moves qigong away from concentration absorption, toward shared, outward attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana withdraws from the senses into one inner object, usually under a teacher's guidance; going the other way, this keeps the eyes open and attention spread across a circle of people moving together, with the timing held by the whole group. Nobody leads, and everyone adjusts.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to ten people who have learned the same short form from a teacher stand in a circle in a park or hall and do it together for about 20 minutes, with no music or counting, letting the pace settle by watching each other. Afterward they stand still for a few minutes with eyes open, then each says in a sentence or two when the group felt together and when it did not.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have learned qigong in classes and want to keep practicing with others without a teacher, and people who find closed-eye practice too inward.
modalities.cautions: The main risks are those of gentle exercise, so adapt movements to your body and keep up any prescribed treatment. Unusual mental or bodily reactions during qigong, such as strong agitation or confusion, are a reason to stop and see a doctor, especially for people with a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: A slow qigong form, done in a circle with eyes open and no teacher at the front: the group keeps time by watching each other. Leaderless Circle Form is an untested idea for shared, outward attention. Learn the form from a teacher first.

modalities.name: Earplugs In, Body Heard
modalities.tagline: Outside sound shut out, the body's own signals noticed.
modalities.whatItIs: Earplugs In, Body Heard is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from dance: no music, no movement and no company. You sit alone with earplugs in, so outside sound fades, and observe the quiet inner sounds and sensations that remain, such as the heartbeat, swallowing and breath, as they arise and pass.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance moves the body to outside music, with other people; going the other way, this stills the body, removes outside sound and company, and turns observation toward the body's own small, changing signals. A fixed schedule keeps it steady.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a day for a week you sit alone for 20 minutes at set times, with soft foam earplugs in, eyes closed and the body still. You do not label or change anything: you observe each inner sound or sensation, a heartbeat, a gulp, the hiss of the breath, until it changes or fades, and then wait for the next.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who find outside noise distracting, and people curious about how much the body is quietly doing all the time.
modalities.cautions: Blocking outside sound can make ringing in the ears or a racing heartbeat more noticeable and, for some, more worrying, so take the earplugs out if that happens, and people with tinnitus, health anxiety or panic should start with very short sits or skip it. Like other insight practice it can bring up difficult experiences, and people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before longer or retreat practice.
modalities.tweet: Earplugs in, eyes closed, 20 minutes. What's left to hear is your own heartbeat, breath and swallowing. Earplugs In, Body Heard is a new meditation idea for watching the body's quiet signals come and go. Untested. Skip it if tinnitus or health worries flare.

modalities.name: Curtains Drawn Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard intervals alone, with no mirror, music or anyone watching.
modalities.whatItIs: Curtains Drawn Intervals is a new, untested idea that pushes interval training away from dance: no music, no partner, no audience and no concern for how you look. You do a fixed, hard interval session alone, with the curtains drawn and no mirror, and judge it only by whether you did the work.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance is social, musical and seen, and it values expression and grace; going the other way, this is solitary, silent and unseen, so effort can be as clumsy, red-faced and noisy as it needs to be. Being unwatched is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: At home, on a stationary bike or with simple moves such as step-ups, you warm up for 10 minutes and follow the same written plan every time: six hard bouts of 30 seconds with 90 seconds easy, timed by a plain beeper. There is no music, mirror or camera, and afterward you record one thing only, whether you completed the plan, then cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who would like to train hard but feel self-conscious in gyms, in classes or anywhere they might be watched.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts put a heavy load on the heart and training alone means nobody is there to help, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems or other conditions, keep a phone within reach, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Start with fewer bouts and build up gradually to avoid strains.
modalities.tweet: Hard training, curtains drawn, nobody watching: no mirror, no music, no class. Curtains Drawn Intervals is a new idea if gyms make you feel watched. Untested. Check with your doctor first if needed, keep your phone near, and stop at any chest pain.

modalities.name: Wrong-Foot Games
modalities.tagline: Pickup games where a good fake counts as much as a goal.
modalities.whatItIs: Wrong-Foot Games is a new, untested idea for a fast pickup game in which faking out an opponent, with a dummy, a feint or a sudden change of pace, earns points alongside ordinary goals. It pushes team sport away from dance: instead of moving in time with others, you practice breaking their timing on purpose, and being fooled in turn.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance builds connection by moving in sync with a partner and the music; going the other way, this plays with surprise and unpredictability between opponents, so reading people and being read becomes a game of quick, good-humored deception. Getting fooled is part of the fun, not a failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, two teams of five to seven play a small-sided ball game on grass for about 45 minutes, with no referee and no music. A fake that makes a defender commit the wrong way earns a point if that defender raises a hand to admit it, and at half-time each player shows their team one fake that worked on them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who take being caught out or surprised very personally, and players who enjoy cheeky, playful competition.
modalities.cautions: Sudden changes of direction raise the risk of knee and ankle injuries, so warm up well, build up gradually, play on even ground and stop playing after any knock to the head. People with heart or other health conditions should get medical advice first, and anyone with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness stops at once.
modalities.tweet: In Wrong-Foot Games, sending a defender the wrong way scores a point, as long as they raise a hand to admit it. A new concept for playful competition where being fooled is part of the fun. Untested. Warm up well, since quick cuts are hard on knees.

modalities.name: The Run Home
modalities.tagline: Running home alone, as the gap between your day and your evening.
modalities.whatItIs: The Run Home is a new, untested idea that pushes endurance training away from dance: no music, no partner, no audience and no plan beyond getting home. Once or twice a week you run home alone from work, school or a station, so the run becomes a private stretch of hard, steady effort between other people's company and your own front door.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance is shared, musical and done for its own sake in a space full of other people; going the other way, this is solitary, unaccompanied effort with a plain, practical destination. The day's people are behind you, home is ahead, and the stretch between is yours alone.
modalities.whatYouDo: You plan a safe route of 30 to 50 minutes, carry only a light pack, and start with five minutes of walking and easy jogging before settling into a steady, fairly hard pace. There are no headphones, no tracking and no stopping to chat, and when you reach home you walk for a few minutes, stretch, then go in.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who go straight from a crowded day into a busy home and want a short, private gap in between, and runners who prefer effort with a purpose.
modalities.cautions: Running hard strains the heart and joints, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems, build up distance gradually and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Running alone on roads means choosing well-lit routes, wearing bright clothing, carrying a phone, telling someone your route and leaving the run for another day in bad weather.
modalities.tweet: After work, run home alone: no headphones, no tracking. The Run Home is a new idea: a private stretch of hard effort between a busy day and a busy house. Untested. Pick a lit route, carry a phone, and build up distance gradually.

modalities.name: One Lift Season
modalities.tagline: One lift, alone, three times a week, for twelve weeks.
modalities.whatItIs: One Lift Season is a new, untested idea that pushes strength training away from dance, toward solitude, repetition and precise, planned change. For twelve weeks you train a single lift alone, three times a week, to a written plan that changes only the weight, in small steps.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance offers variety, music, company and self-expression; going the other way, this strips training down to one movement done alone until it is thoroughly known, so progress is easy to see and nothing else competes for attention. The plan, not the mood of the day, decides each session.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose one lift with a qualified coach, such as the squat, deadlift or bench press, and learn it well before starting. Each session you warm up, do the planned sets, for example 5 sets of 5 with 2 to 3 minutes of rest, add a small fixed amount of weight whenever every set is completed with good form, and write down only the weight and whether the sets were done.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel scattered and want one clear, measurable thing to get better at, and lifters who enjoy routine more than variety.
modalities.cautions: Training one lift hard for weeks can overload the same joints and muscles, so warm up every time, add only small amounts of weight, take an easy week when needed, keep breathing rather than holding your breath and use safety bars or a spotter. People with high blood pressure or heart, back or joint problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Twelve weeks, one lift, three times a week, a little more weight each time. One Lift Season is an untested idea for anyone who feels scattered and wants one clear thing to get better at. Learn the lift from a coach first, and keep breathing under the bar.

modalities.name: Know Each Hen
modalities.tagline: Quiet bench time in a hen run, learning to tell hens apart.
modalities.whatItIs: Know Each Hen is a new, untested idea for calm, one-to-one sessions in which you sit still on a bench inside a hen run with a trained professional and slowly learn to tell six to eight hens apart by their markings, gait and habits. It pushes animal-assisted work away from dance: no movement, music or crowd, only quiet, careful looking and a few words.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance is lively, musical and shared through moving bodies; going the other way, this is stillness, quiet and close attention, aimed at seeing each animal as an individual rather than as one of a flock. Telling them apart is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for about 45 minutes you sit on a bench in the run while the hens go about their day, and the professional helps you notice details such as comb shape, feather patterns, who dust-bathes and who keeps to the edge. You quietly say what you notice, and over several weeks you see how many hens you can name on sight; the hens are not picked up or hand-fed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel unseen or lumped in with everyone else, or who want a very calm, low-pressure way to practice patient attention.
modalities.cautions: Hens can carry germs such as salmonella, so wash your hands after each session, and people with allergies, a weakened immune system or a fear of birds should say so first. The hens must always have space, shelter and freedom to move away, and the professional ends a session if they seem stressed.
modalities.tweet: Sit on a bench in a hen run and slowly learn to tell every hen apart: comb, feathers, who bathes in dust, who keeps to the edge. Know Each Hen is a quiet new concept for practicing patient attention. Untested. Wash your hands after.

modalities.name: Half-Speed Rounds
modalities.tagline: The same short form, each round twice as slow.
modalities.whatItIs: Half-Speed Rounds is a new, untested idea that pushes qigong away from dance: no music, no beat, no company and no improvisation. You repeat one short, set form alone, and each round you do it at half the speed of the round before, until the movement is barely visible.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance follows a beat with other people and invites free expression; going the other way, this drops the beat altogether and stretches time inside a fixed form, practiced alone. As the movement slows, attention has more and more room to rest on it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing alone in a quiet room, you do a short form of four or five movements learned from a teacher, first in about 1 minute, then in 2, then 4, then 8, for about 15 minutes of movement in all. You finish by standing still for a few minutes, and you add no music, counting or changes to the form.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rush through everything, including their calming practices, and want a simple, structured way to slow down.
modalities.cautions: The risks are mainly those of gentle exercise, though moving very slowly on bent knees can tire the legs, so keep a chair nearby and adapt the movements to your body. Unusual mental or bodily reactions during qigong, such as strong agitation, confusion or strange perceptions, are a reason to stop and see a doctor, especially for people with a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Do a short qigong form in one minute. Then in two, then four, then eight. Half-Speed Rounds is a new idea: the same few movements, each round twice as slow, until they barely look like movement at all. Untested and very simple.
